newsitem.title: USA: Study links Prozac to minor birth abnormalities.
newsitem.headline: Study links Prozac to minor birth abnormalities.

text.p: Prozac, the most commonly used depression-fighting drug in the United States, may cause several minor abnormalities in a baby if the mother takes it during pregnancy, a new study has concluded.
But the results, published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, were greeted with some scepticism.

Previous studies have failed to uncover any problems when Prozac is taken during pregnancy. Other factors, such as the way the women were selected for the study and the other medicines they were taking at the same time as Prozac, may have been responsible for the findings.

Nonetheless, the charity March of Dimes, issued an immediate call to pregnant women and those planning to become pregnant to try to avoid taking Prozac. "The higher rate of prematurity among the babies of women in this study who took Prozac in the last trimester of pregnancy is troubling," Dr. Richard Johnson, medical director of the charity, said.

A team led by Christina D. Chambers of the University of California, San Diego, selected 228 women taking Prozac from about 500 pregnant women who called a birth-defects hotline seeking information about the drug. They used 254 other pregnant callers who were not taking Prozac as a control.
The Chambers group found Prozac did not cause miscarriages or any major deformities, such as heart defects or cleft palates.

But the drug, also known by its generic name fluoxetine and sold by Eli Lilly and Co., seemed to increase the likelihood that a mother who takes it during the first three months of her pregnancy will give birth to a child with minor structural abnormalities, such as underdeveloped fingernails or an extra fold of skin in the inner corner of the eye.

They found 15.5 percent of the women in the Prozac group whose babies were examined for minor problems had at least three of them, which the Chambers team called "an unusual finding." But 6.5 percent of the women in the control group fell into that category as well.
The researchers did not find a link between the drug and any particular type of abnormality or anomaly.
In a telephone interview, Chambers said, "We really don't know what this means, but it raises attention to the possible long-term effects."
She added that when a substance caused anomalies, one generally saw a pattern. "There was no pattern here."
When Prozac was taken during the last three months of pregnancy, there was a higher risk of premature delivery, having the jitters and other problems, the researchers said.

But in an editorial in the journal, Dr. Elisabeth Robert of the European Institute of Genetic Mutations in Lyon, France, said the results of the new study might have been skewed by the decision to find patients through the birth-defects hotine.
In addition, the depression that led to the use of Prozac may have contributed to the results, and the women in the Prozac group tended to be older and thus more likely to have babies with defects.

Robert also said the findings might be explained by the fact that "prematurity, admission to a special-care nursery and poor neonatal adaptation are known to be associated with psychiatric disorders in the mother."
Robert noted that 30 percent of the Prozac users were also taking other drugs -- another possible cause of the defects.

As five previous studies have found no such problems, she said "it seems unjustified to use these new results as a reason to withhold fluoxetine from women who require an antidepressant drug during pregnancy."
Prozac is taken by more than 12 million people worldwide.
